[0:18] knows that the fight against Xerxes  begins that day, but feels only a grim  
[0:24] (if calm) impatience to check the arrogant  hoards that would presume to conquer all.  
[0:31] The Great King Xerxes observes the stubborn  several thousand Greeks arrayed for battle,  
[0:37] perhaps confident his vast army will quickly  sweep aside their pitiful defences and send  
[0:43] them scurrying back into the lands he would  soon rule. Greek blood would redden the earth,  
[0:51] these insolent peoples would bend the knee and  his father’s defeat at Marathon would be avenged.  
[1:00] The ground shakes as the first wave of warriors  approaches the Allied phalanx. The war for Sparta  
[1:07] and for all of Free Greece was on. As with many great events of history,  
[1:18] the events surrounding Leonidas, Xerxes and  their armies’ iconic struggle at Thermopylae can  
[1:24] be directly traced to the earlier defeat of the  First Persian Invasion that commenced in 492 BC.   
[1:34] During the reign of Xerxes’ father Darius, the  Persian Empire had launched a largely successful  
[1:39] invasion in response to Greek interference in the  Ionian Revolt, which saw Darius re-conquer Thrace,  
[1:47] subjugate Macedon to his will and solidify  Persian dominance over the Aegean Sea.   
[1:55] However, though largely successful in  its objectives, the invasion failed to  
[2:00] incorporate all of the Greek lands into  the king of kings’ vast domain. Indeed,  
[2:07] around a decade before Thermopylae at Marathon,  the allied army of Athens and Plataea defeated the  
[2:14] invaders and denied the Persians mainland Greece. Even so, the presence of Persianized Thrace and  
[2:22] Macedon so close to their own homes could not  have soothed concerns of those free cities that  
[2:29] the king of kings’ designs were truly checked. The Persian or Achaemenid Empire was truly the  
[2:37] superpower of the age. Having its origins in  the rise of Cyrus the Great. The domain of the  
[2:44] Great Kings covered an area from Egypt to the  Indus, from the Aral Sea to Macedon on the very  
[2:51] doorstep of the Greek states themselves. Darius’ empire was vastly more powerful  
[2:58] in resources and men and the King  of Kings now set to the task of  
[3:02] organising his overland campaign to finish  the defiant Greeks states once and for all.  
[3:10] Alas for Darius, this was not to be. Having passed  away in 486, Xerxes assumed his father’s place and  
[3:19] inherited the ambition of subduing the Greeks. A  revolt in Egypt in 486 delayed this, but by 481  
[3:28] Xerxes’ own preparations were well underway.  As well as the pontoon bridges and a canal,  
[3:35] supply depots dotting the Thracian and Macedonian  coastlines left the defiant Greeks in no doubt  
[3:42] that the reckoning was fast approaching. So who was this new king of kings bent on  
[3:49] avenging his father? Xerxes was the first  son born to Darius following his own rise  
[3:54] to power. His own lineage was impressive, not  only as the son of the reigning Great King  
[4:01] but no less than a maternal grandson of Cyrus  the Great himself, through his mother Atossa.  
[4:08] Darius obviously held high hopes for his tall  and handsome younger son as Xerxes was made heir  
[4:14] apparent over his elder half-brother Artabazanes.  Undoubtedly noting that his predecessors had  
[4:22] conquered before him to solidify their grip on the  throne, for Xerxes then the pressure was doubly  
[4:28] so given his rise to the throne was through  selection rather than strict primogeniture.  
[4:36] Far from a coward or weakling as implied from  a reading of Herodotus, as a King of Kings,  
[4:42] Xerxes by definition was a warrior endorsed by  a warrior elite, the succession running from  
[4:49] father to son. Having subdued the Egyptians  and perhaps the Babylonians too in 485,  
[4:57] Xerxes also campaigned in Africa and Asia.  All this flies in the face of the cliché  
[5:04] effeminate caricature of the eastern despot. As for the other great figure of Thermopylae,  
[5:12] King Leonidas couldn’t have been more different.  As the leading state, and most powerful of  
[5:19] the alliance, Sparta could thus arguably  boast supreme status in the Greek world.  
[5:26] At the time of Thermopylae, King Leonidas ruled  as the Agiad monarch. Around the age of sixty  
[5:34] at Thermopylae, Leonidas had not long reigned  as king, only having assumed the title nine  
[5:40] years before. As the third of four sons born to  Anaxandridas II, Leonidas likely never expected to  
[5:48] become king, though – married to Gorgo, daughter  of Cleomenes – he was well-placed to do so after  
[5:55] the dodgy demise of his elder half-brother. Prevented from mobilising their full army due to  
[6:03] the taboo of doing so during the yearly festival  in Apollo’s honour, this then was the king who led  
[6:09] the famous three hundred out of Sparta to jointly  face the oncoming wrath of the Persians in 480.  
[6:18] Given his age of around sixty, it’s quite likely  Leonidas’ military experience was grounded in the  
[6:25] smaller conflicts that were typical of his time. While opposition to the Persians was focused on  
[6:32] Sparta and her Peloponnesian allies,  the joint-victors of Marathon, Athens,  
[6:37] obviously had a vested interest in resistance,  given they were to be given particular attention  
[6:44] by Xerxes and so also joined this alliance,  to form the Hellenic League, which was further  
[6:51] bolstered by various other cities and islands. Thessaly too had initially elected to fight,  
[6:59] and in that spirit reinforced a hoplite  force that would contest the Persians at  
[7:04] the Vale of Tempe. However, upon learning  the true extent of their foe’s numbers  
[7:11] and realising this position was untenable,  had little choice but to yield to Xerxes.  
[7:18] The remaining allies thus zeroed in  on Thermopylae to make their stand,  
[7:23] while at sea the Hellenic fleet would hold  position to the east off the north of the  
[7:27] island of Euboia to contest the Persians. The army that Xerxes had gathered at Sardis  
[7:35] in the autumn of 481 was indeed massive  by any estimation. To the Greeks,  
[7:42] even the modern conservative estimates  of eighty thousand that made up the total  
[7:47] number of the Persian army would have seemed  gigantic. Though Herodotus’ total strength  
[7:53] of over five million is grossly overinflated,  then, a Persian force of upwards of the lower  
[8:00] hundreds of thousands was more than enough  to crush Greek resistance once and for all.  
[8:07] With the onset of Spring, Xerxes’ colossal  army lumbered west across the Hellespont  
[8:13] and towards central Greece through the  vassal countries of Thrace and Macedonia.   
[8:20] At sea, the Greek fleet held its position  about forty miles east of the army,  
[8:26] set to halt any Persian attempt to turn the land  forces. It’s likely too that the fleet here also  
[8:34] sought to prevent a full Persian takeover of  Euboia, from which there was a short jump across  
[8:40] the narrow straight into Attica and Boeotia. Luckily for the Greek fleet, the superior Persian  
[8:48] fleet was mauled by a storm en route to the area  off of the coast of Magnesia. Having spied their  
[8:56] Greek foes from their temporary base of Aphetai,  the Persians decided to send a detachment to round  
[9:04] Euboia and cut off the Artemisia fleet. This force  of ships too, however, was caught in a storm off  
[9:11] the eastern shores of the island, while the Greeks  had sailed to engage the remaining Persians.  
[9:19] Fighting a fierce days-long engagement with the  reduced Persian fleet, the allies too had taken  
[9:25] significant losses, though the Persians too had  suffered. However, unable to afford these losses  
[9:33] unlike the Persians, the Greek fleet withdrew to  Salamis to await better circumstances to fight.  
[9:41] Meanwhile on land, Leonidas was readying his men  at Thermopylae. Though famously narrow in general,  
[9:49] the level passage squashed between  the mountains to the left and the  
[9:53] sea to the right was particularly narrow at  three points: the so-called East and West  
[9:59] Gates were particularly narrow, while the Middle  Gate – though wider – had other advantages.  
[10:06] This point in the pass, formidably guarded the  left flank of the holding force with a sizable  
[10:12] sheer cliff, whereas the other gates landward  approaches were merely steep but not sheer.  
[10:19] A further plus for Leonidas was the presence of  the Phocian Wall. Though somewhat in disrepair,  
[10:26] a wall had been constructed by the Phocians to  help contest the invasions of their enemies the  
[10:32] Thessalians. The day before the commencement  of battle, Leonidas set his men to repairing  
[10:38] it as best they could, though only so much  could be done about the major disadvantage  
[10:43] of trying to check the Persians in this area.  The Anopaia Path did present a way around the  
[10:51] allied position, however, as with all invasions  in a time where maps were rare if non-existent,  
[10:58] such local knowledge was beyond the foreign force.  To guard the path, the Spartan monarch dispatched  
[11:05] about a thousand Phocians; these local men  certainly had the most to immediately lose and,  
[11:12] in theory, were likely to sell their  lives dearly to any would-be aggressor.  
[13:12] As for the enemy, Xerxes’ vast army arrived  at the battlefield four days before the first  
[13:19] blood of battle. In that time Herodotus famously  relates how a Persian scout spied the Spartans  
[13:26] calmly combing their hair or working out near to  the Phocian Wall. On asking his advisor Demaratos  
[13:34] what this was all about, the exiled Spartan king  signalled this was a Spartan battle preparation.   
[13:41] Though bizarre to the Great King, the wearing of  their hair long was actually a privilege granted  
[13:47] on reaching manhood, alongside the more famous  donning of the red cloak. Preferring this style  
[13:55] due to the belief it made them appear taller and  thus more imposing in battle, it’s little wonder  
[14:00] then that Xerxes’ spy sighted the Spartan Homoioi  meticulously combing and oiling their locks.  
[14:09] During this lull before the storm, Xerxes  also sent another envoy to the Greeks to  
[14:14] lay down their arms, to which the Spartan  monarch laconically replied in true Spartan  
[14:20] fashion: molon labe – “come and get them!”  This impertinent reply may have finally spurred

[14:41] meagre army may have astonished and angered  the Great King in equal measure. It’s likely  
[14:49] his delay had been to merely await the dawning  of reality on Leonidas and his doomed comrades.  
[14:56] With no meek withdrawal forthcoming the King  of Kings ordered his Median and Kissian forces  
[15:03] forward to clear the way. As intended the  superior numbers did little to tilt the  
[15:10] scales of fortune in Xerxes’ favour. Of course,  no small amount of bravery and determination also  
[15:18] aided the defenders; another factor to success,  however, was the way in which the Greeks fought.  
[15:25] Xerxes by attacking this way was allowing  the Greeks to fight the battle their way,  
[15:31] spear-to-spear, eyeball-to-eyeball. The Greek  style of fighting common to all the levy citizen  
[15:39] soldiers of the poleis was the phalanx formation,  the tight and near-unstoppable mass of men,  
[15:46] shields and spears that was ideal  for defending the narrow terrain.  
[15:53] Factor into matters the hoplite soldier’s  panoply: a man would wear the Corinthian-style  
[15:58] bronze helmet, while his torso would have  been covered by his wide aspis shield;  
[16:04] bronze greaves protected the lower legs of the  combatant, while on the offensive side of things,  
[16:10] the long spear (of around two to two-and-a-half  metres long) out-reached the average Persian’s.  
[16:18] Further protected by a coat of bronze or linen,  in contrast to the average Persian assailant,  
[16:24] it’s little wonder why Leonidas’ allied army was  so deadly over those three days of bloody mêlée.  
[16:33] The Medes and Kissians would mostly be equipped  with a smaller spear and a wicker oval-shaped  
[16:39] shield in the main. In addition, most Persian  infantry would also wield a composite bow with  
[16:45] a quiver of iron-tipped reed arrows.  In addition to the usual double-bladed

[16:59] Of these weapons, the bow was undoubtedly  the ‘national’ weapon, so to speak,  
[17:04] and even a symbol associated with the Persian  kings. Indeed, in previous conflicts masses of  
[17:11] volleys were often used to clear enemy formations,  yet on this first day at Thermopylae Xerxes’  
[17:18] mêlée-focused approach had led to severe losses. Part of the Greek strategy ahead of the wall was  
[17:26] to feign retreat, only to quickly halt and turn  on their pursuers. This rapid escalation of hopes  
[17:35] and collapse of progress must have taken its toll  on Persian morale, alongside the mounting bodies  
[17:42] of their comrades. By keeping the battle a  mobile affair, Leonidas was also cleverly  
[17:48] mitigating the deadly effect of the Persian  archers, denying his foes a fixed target.  
[17:56] Having beaten off this first series of assaults,  Leonidas must have thanked the Gods that Xerxes  
[18:02] impatiently ordered his best men forward to  engage in the later afternoon. Perhaps the king  
[18:09] appreciated that his army was still relatively  fresh; better now than to face Xerxes’ elite when  
[18:16] wounds and weariness were worse for his men. The Immortals, as the Greeks named them,

[18:29] these elite professionals presented the  best Xerxes had to offer, while within these  
[18:35] ten thousand so-called ‘silver-butted’ infantry  also marched the so-called ‘gold-butted’ elite  
[18:42] within an elite: one thousand of the noblest and  bravest of the Immortals. Known as the ‘King’s  
[18:49] spear-bearers’ but also colloquially referred  to as ‘apple-bearers’ due to the golden-shaped  
[18:55] butts of their short spears, this inner-most  personal guard of the Great King were formed  
[19:02] from the noble class, the other nine thousand  picked as the cream of the commoners.   
[19:09] Led by Hydarnes, in the event – despite their own  fearsome reputation and on paper outnumbering the  
[19:16] entire Greek force that day – the Immortals  could not dislodge Leonidas and his comrades.  
[19:25] Having fought off the initial  waves and then Xerxes best,  
[19:29] Leonidas may have allowed himself a brief window  to hope that his army could hold indefinitely or  
[19:36] long enough for Xerxes to rethink his approach.  The second day of fighting was similar to the  
[19:42] first. The Great King’s men fell on the Greek  formations like waves upon a rock, however,  
[19:50] as in nature so too with war: over time though  relatively fewer in number the Greeks inevitably  
[19:58] took wounds and losses, the solid rock  of defence inevitably slowly eroding.  
[20:05] Herodotus informs us that the Greeks fought in  relays, so that much – if not the majority – of  
[20:11] the hard fighting must have been done by  those non-Spartiates present. Perhaps, then,  
[20:18] Leonidas held back at times in grim respect  for his allies, though undoubtedly at other  
[20:24] times the sixty-year-old monarch would have been  in the thick of things in true Homeric style.  
[20:31] This period must have been frustrating for Xerxes.  Likely observing events from an elevated position,  
[20:39] his numbers and threats had done little to  advance his cause. What he really needed to  
[20:44] change his fortunes was decent local knowledge  of either an alternative route into mainland  
[20:50] Greece or a means to clear the obvious route  in front of him. Enter one of the more infamous

[21:05] for a suitably grand reward from the Great King –  offered to lead enemy soldiers along the mountain  
[21:12] path that would allow Xerxes’ men to take the  Greeks in the rear. Leaving nothing to chance,  
[21:19] Xerxes sent all of his Immortals with  Ephialtes, their only block en route  
[21:26] being the unseen thousand-strong Phocian  contingent. Herodotus indicates all the  
[21:33] remaining Immortals made the march, which means  the guardian army of Greeks must have been  
[21:39] heavily outnumbered many times over. Having marched through the night,  
[21:45] Hydarnes and the Immortals closed in on  the Phocian position. Equally shocked,  
[21:51] the Immortals loosed their arrows. The Phocians,  though brave, mistakenly believed themselves to be  
[21:58] the intended target of the Persian elite  and retired to some high ground to exact  
[22:04] a bloody price for their deaths. In response, the  disciplined ranks of the Immortals merely bypassed  
[22:12] them and continued towards the East Gate. Leonidas learned his fate was sealed with the  
[22:20] coming of deserters in the night, the news  of the Persian manoeuvre being confirmed by  
[22:25] his own lookouts just after dawn. Taking council  again, Leonidas sent the majority of the remaining  
[22:33] Greeks away, electing to remain with the three  hundred (or what was left of them), as well as  
[22:40] seven hundred Thespians and four hundred Thebans. On the surface, modern audiences may wonder why  
[22:49] Leonidas – faced with such a hopeless  situation – didn’t simply withdraw all  
[22:54] his army and fight another day? According  to Herodotus, the Spartan king had his own  
[23:01] reasons for remaining himself. According to  the Oracle at Delphi, either Sparta would  
[23:07] be laid waste, or a king of Sparta would fall. The Persian pincer would close on Leonidas and his  
[23:15] remaining men between nine and ten in the morning,  though unsurprisingly – given the difficulty of  
[23:22] exactly coordinating such an action – Hydarnes and  the Immortals were late in coming up the rear.  
[23:30] Unlike on the previous days in which the Greeks  fought in relays at the narrowest point of the  
[23:35] Middle Gate, Leonidas now moved his position  forward to contest the Persians in a wider area,  
[23:42] the better to fully deploy his remaining  forces. Advancing in good order at first, as  
[23:49] the Greeks closed with the Persians, the latter’s  volleys must have undoubtedly done some damage.  
[23:56] Breaking with normal custom, Leonidas then ordered  an all-out charge, and it was now that desperate  
[24:03] fighting broke out, the king himself at the  forefront. By quickly advancing on a wider front,  
[24:10] the arrows may have inflicted less damage  than otherwise; conversely the Persian  
[24:16] losses were said to have exceeded those  of the previous two days. It was around  
[24:21] this time that Leonidas likely roared his last  battle-cry and fell among many of his comrades.  
[24:30] A furious battle over possession of the king’s  body now ensued; the surviving Greeks ferociously  
[24:36] pushed back the Persians four times before they  regained possession. The sheer desperation of the  
[24:44] last fighting was related to by Herodotus,  writing that when Greek spears were broken,  
[24:51] they wielded their swords and when they too were  lost they resorted to using their hands and teeth.  
[24:59] Despite this last grim success, however, the  inevitable loomed with the final approach  
[25:05] of the Immortals from the rear.  Upon realising the time was near,  
[25:11] the Greeks withdrew through the Phocian Wall and  redeployed on a hillock to await their final fate.  
[25:20] At this point too, the Thebans’ resolve finally  broke as they broke off from the Spartans and  
[25:26] the Thespians, fleeing towards the Persian  lines. Many were slaughtered in a blood rage,  
[25:33] though most offers of surrender were  taken. These fortunate men were later  
[25:38] branded with Xerxes mark for their troubles. With the Immortals also finally upon them,  
[25:46] the Phocian wall breached, the enemy decided to  wisely finish those surviving Greeks with a storm  
[25:53] of arrows. So ended the battle at Thermopylae. With the fall of Leonidas and his rearguard,  
[26:04] Thermopylae began its long history as arguably  the icon of the famous last stand. However,  
[26:11] though the battle cemented the Spartan  legacy in the pages of history,  
[26:15] their glorious last stand would have been of  limited comfort to the inhabitants of Lokris,  
[26:21] Boeotia and Attica. Xerxes would  not soon forget Leonidas or his  
[26:28] estimated twenty thousand losses at Thermopylae  and would exact appropriate retribution.  
[26:35] Athens was burned, though its population had been  evacuated. At sea, the free Greeks were far from  
[26:43] vanquished. Though defeated at Artemision,  they scored a decisive victory at Salamis,  
[26:50] which forced the withdrawal of the Persian fleet  back to Anatolia. As for the Great King himself,  
[26:58] he returned home too, leaving the bulk of his  land forces to finish business in Greece.  
[27:05] Alas for Mardonius, the would-be-satrap of  a conquered Greece, his star would fall soon  
[27:12] after. Gathering the largest army seen up to  that point, nearly forty thousand hoplites –  
[27:19] Spartans included – the Greeks defeated the  Persians at Plataea, freeing themselves from  
[27:26] the threat of Persian subjugation for good. The defeat of the second Persian invasion of  
[27:33] Greece did much to foster a wider ethnic and  cultural sense of Greek identity as contrasted  
[27:40] with barbarian folk. In Athens especially the  conflict was framed as an ideological struggle,  
[27:48] the Greeks representing freedom over  tyranny, a view of the conflict that  
[27:53] largely persists in the western public  consciousness down to the present day.
